subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Psychology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the independent variable (IV) in an experiment?
options: The variable that is manipulated or changed by the researcher
A variable that is kept constant
questions.explain: The independent variable is the variable the researcher manipulates or changes; the dependent variable is the one that is measured.

questions.q: In a study where half of participants rehearse a word list and half do not, and recall is then measured, what is the dependent variable?
questions.explain: The dependent variable is the number of words recalled, because that is what is measured; rehearsal condition is the independent variable.

questions.q: The age or memory ability of participants that could accidentally affect results is an example of which type of extraneous variable?
questions.explain: Characteristics of the participants themselves, such as age or ability, are participant variables; features of the setting are situational variables.

questions.q: Using the same instructions and conditions for every participant is an example of which control?
questions.explain: Standardised procedures keep instructions and conditions the same for all participants, helping control situational extraneous variables.

questions.q: In which technique do neither the participants nor the researcher interacting with them know which condition participants are in?
questions.explain: In a double-blind technique, neither the participants nor the researcher running the study knows the condition, reducing bias from both.

questions.q: Which statement is a null hypothesis?
options: There will be no difference in recall between the two conditions; any difference is due to chance
Older people will recall more words
questions.explain: A null hypothesis predicts no difference (or relationship) between variables, stating any difference found is due to chance.

questions.q: Which of these is an alternative (experimental) hypothesis?
options: There will be no difference between the groups
Participants who rehearse will recall significantly more words than those who do not
Any difference is due to chance
questions.explain: An alternative hypothesis predicts a difference or relationship between the variables, here that rehearsal increases recall.

questions.q: A researcher asks the first 10 people they meet in a cafe to take part. Which sampling method is this?
questions.explain: Selecting whoever is available and willing at the time is opportunity sampling; it is quick but can be unrepresentative.

questions.q: Recruiting participants who reply to a newspaper advert (as in Zimbardo's prison study) is an example of which sampling method?
questions.explain: Participants who respond to an advertisement are self-selecting, which is volunteer sampling; it can attract an unrepresentative, keen sample.

questions.q: Which sampling method gives every member of the target population an equal chance of being chosen, for example by drawing names from a hat?
questions.explain: Random sampling gives every member of the target population an equal chance of selection, reducing researcher bias.

questions.q: In which experimental design do the same participants take part in every condition?
questions.explain: In a repeated measures design the same participants take part in all conditions, which controls for participant variables but risks order effects.

questions.q: A researcher uses different participants in each condition and pairs them on age and IQ. Which design is this?
questions.explain: Pairing different participants on key characteristics before allocating them to conditions is a matched pairs design.

questions.q: Which UK body publishes the ethical guidelines that psychologists follow?
questions.explain: The British Psychological Society (BPS) publishes the codes of ethics and conduct that guide psychological research in the UK.

questions.q: A researcher publishes participants' names alongside their results on a website. Which ethical guideline has been broken?
questions.explain: Publishing identifiable data breaks confidentiality; participants' data should be kept private and anonymous.

questions.q: Telling participants they may leave the study at any point without penalty respects which ethical guideline?
questions.explain: The right to withdraw means participants can leave at any time, without penalty, and can withdraw their data.

questions.q: A study manipulates an IV in a highly controlled, artificial setting. Which method and strength does this describe?
options: A laboratory experiment, high control and internal validity
A case study, in-depth qualitative data
A field experiment, high ecological validity
questions.explain: A laboratory experiment manipulates the IV in a controlled setting, giving high control and internal validity but possibly low ecological validity.

questions.q: What does the 'reliability' of a study refer to?
options: Whether it measures what it claims to measure
Whether it produces consistent results if repeated
questions.explain: Reliability refers to consistency: whether the same results would be obtained if the study were repeated. Validity is about measuring what is intended.

questions.q: Detailed written descriptions of participants' feelings are an example of what type of data?
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical, such as written accounts of feelings; quantitative data is numerical.

questions.q: For the scores 15, 11, 10, 13, 18, 19, 14, what is the median?
questions.explain: Ordered: 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 18, 19. The middle (4th of 7) value is 14, so the median is 14.

questions.q: On a scatter diagram, as scores on one variable increase, scores on the other decrease. What does this show?
questions.explain: When one variable rises as the other falls, the scatter diagram shows a negative correlation. Correlation does not prove cause and effect.
